content: Once the paroxysmal cough phase of pertussis is established, antimicrobial treatment is primarily used to eradicate Bordetella pertussis and prevent its transmission. Without effective antimicrobial therapy, B. pertussis can persist in infants for six weeks or longer and in adults and adolescents for 21 days or more. Detailed guidelines for post-exposure antimicrobial prophylaxis and treatment of pertussis have been previously published. Pregnant women with pertussis near term and other household contacts with pertussis are significant sources of infection for newborn infants. Antimicrobial treatment and prophylaxis are effective in preventing the transmission of pertussis to neonates. Macrolides are administered to pregnant women who acquire pertussis late in pregnancy or shortly before delivery, as well as to their household contacts and the neonate. Early recognition of pertussis in pregnant women is critical to ensure the effectiveness of this approach. Pregnancy is not a contraindication for the use of erythromycin, azithromycin, or clarithromycin. Erythromycin and azithromycin are classified as FDA Category B drugs, while clarithromycin is classified as a Category C drug. Macrolides can interact with various other therapeutic agents, which may preclude their concurrent use. Adverse effects, such as hepatic dysfunction or pseudomembranous colitis, are rare. Infants under one month of age who receive erythromycin are at increased risk for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS). Due to this risk and the fact that azithromycin is associated with fewer adverse effects than erythromycin, azithromycin is the preferred antimicrobial for prophylaxis in neonates exposed to pertussis. However, there have been reports of IHPS in two preterm infants who received azithromycin for post-exposure prophylaxis. A causal relationship between azithromycin and IHPS has not been established. The mechanisms of immunity to pertussis are not fully understood. Both humoral and cellular immunity are believed to play complementary roles in protection. Immunity resulting from B. pertussis infection or vaccination typically lasts for 5–10 years or more but wanes over time, leaving individuals susceptible to infection or reinfection. Immune responses to B. pertussis can target various toxins and antigens. No specific antibody level, presence of specific antibodies, or antibody profile has been universally accepted as a quantifiable serologic measure of protection. Studies on the use of parenterally administered immune globulins for post-exposure prophylaxis or treatment of pertussis have yielded mixed results and do not clarify the role of passive antibodies in prevention or treatment. These findings also do not predict the role of transplacental maternal antibodies in infant protection. Pertussis toxin (PT), previously known as lymphocytosis-promoting factor (LPF), is considered one of the most clinically relevant toxins and virulence factors of B. pertussis. Detoxified PT is a component of all pertussis vaccines. The pediatric DTaP vaccine containing detoxified PT as the sole immunizing antigen has demonstrated a preventive efficacy of 71% against classical pertussis. However, the contribution of anti-PT antibodies to protection varies across studies. Elevated concentrations of anti-pertactin (PRN) and anti-fimbriae (FIM) antibodies have been most closely associated with protection in household studies and other research. Evidence for additional protection from anti-filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA) antibodies has been mixed. Cell-mediated immune mechanisms are essential for clearing B. pertussis from macrophages and other cells. In addition to humoral responses, B. pertussis antigens in acellular pertussis vaccines induce cell-mediated immune responses after primary immunization with pediatric DTaP in infants, after booster vaccination in children, and after booster vaccination with reduced-antigen-content vaccines in adolescents and adults. Protection is maintained in children whose antibody levels decline below detectable levels over time, suggesting that cell-mediated immunity is a critical component of long-term protection. Cell-mediated immune responses remain measurable for substantially longer periods than antibody responses to the same antigens, particularly PT. These responses to initial doses of pertussis vaccines are believed to correlate better with long-term immunity than antibody responses. Studies since the 1930s have assessed the prevalence of pertussis-specific antibodies in maternal and infant sera using various assays. Detectable pertussis-specific antibodies have been identified in unvaccinated women without a history of pertussis, women with a past history of pertussis, women likely vaccinated with whole-cell pertussis vaccines during childhood, and women with a recent history of pertussis. Most pregnant women, except those with recent pertussis, have low geometric mean concentrations (GMCs) of anti-PT and other pertussis-specific antibodies, consistent with generally low antibody concentrations among adults in the general population. The efficiency of maternal-fetal transfer of IgG antibodies to pertussis-specific antigens varies. Most studies report similar antigen-specific concentrations in cord or neonatal sera and maternal sera measured late in pregnancy or at delivery. However, higher concentrations in cord or neonatal sera compared to maternal sera have been reported, suggesting active transport in certain settings.
